searchText: <@552133098075193354> In my latest PR I changed some variable names per requests and previous discussions. I went with the ultra verbose and specific: `max_fee_per_gas` (previously `fee_cap_per_gas`) `max_inclusion_fee_per_gas` (previously `max_miner_bribe`) `inclusion_fee_per_gas` (previously `effective_miner_bribe`) `effective_gas_price` (what `GASPRICE` opcode is set to) We never did settle on a name, but I think those ones were generally positively received and `bribe` has gotten a lot of hate (and I have been convinced it isn't accurate). Good feedback from the mining channel. What do people think about updating the EIP rationale related to the burning of the base fee? EIPs are technical standards. It is not appropriate to include arguments in them at all. (if such exist now, we should probably remove them) Motivation section is a bit of an exception, as we usually allow some *very high level* statements about why someone would want to implement the EIP. However, it isn't meant to be a constantly updating arguments for/against. "Additionally, this burn counterbalances Ethereum inflation without greatly diminishing miner rewards." <-- that sentence is not really accurate anymore though. The EIP-1559 does already address the hypothetical (well, not anymore I guess) case of transaction rewards being a significant chunk of the total rewards, and why this is undesirable. I'm fine with removing that sentence entirely. <@!301186049323958275> where should a "justification" document live? I'm happy to take a stab at "Why 1559?" but not sure where to have that long-term so folks can easily find it. is it true to say that after 1559, miners will no longer have control of the block target? e.g. today if miners want to include more txs, they can ramp up the block limit by 1% for each tx - with 1559 that block limit increase comes at the cost of the base fee increasing From what I can tell, the gas target can still change (albeit not too much at a time). The basefee is changed based on the parent gas target and parent gas used. The basefee increase is always a function of `parent_gas_used / parent_gas_target` agreed, the gas target can change, but is it true to say that it can change with all else being equal? for example, suppose the initial base fee is 1 nano eth and the first 1559 block gas target is 12.5 mm - can we ever get to a point where we have a block with a larger target (say 20mm) but a base fee 1 nano eth? <@!543900561460822016> yes: miners can still increase the block size post-1559, and the base fee is calculated based on that So, for example, the current block size is 12.5M, post-1559, it means we can have blocks up to 25M (during which the base fee goes up 12.5%). Miners could raise the gas limit to 15M, which would require a 30M block to raise the base fee 12.5% yes i realize this, but that is slightly different than raising the gas limit today because today it doesn't come at the cost of higher fees so theoretically, miners can increase the limit to 100mm Dos becomes likely in 1559, to increase to 100mm there would need to be demand for to grow to this size which is created by the lowering of the basefee Yes that is correct. Minimum viable security for maximally sustained in the moment throughout. Also larger blocks become easier with access lists. I don't really understand why the entire gas limit can grow 2x in 1559. state averages out, but computation and bandwidth is consumed in the instant. if XX gas of computation per block is possible, why not keep it all the time? so it's fair to say that miners lose their ability to control the block limit with 1559 - the target is driven by actual demand and ether being spent? Because state will balloon beyond applicable fees to maintain storage costs. yes but that's what I meant. state should be treated separately See this: https://notes.ethereum.org/@vbuterin/eip_1559_spikes TL;DR: so few blocks are actually "200% full" that it doesn't affect the long-run averages. Should, sure, isn’t though. so you have a constant limit of computation-gas of eg. 20M and eip 1559-style state gas yes but averages only matter for state, and block size itself I suppose. having less computation in the future doesn't pay for more computation in the past Averages matter for the DoS risks and hardware requirements too only full sync no? If all the blocks are 2x as big, any potential attack will be 2x as worse, and nodes will need to process twice as much computation *every* 15 sec vs. occasionally Once nodes have fast sync'ed they process all the blocks at head well ok but that means blocks that need eg. 3 sec to execute are still ok well, what we've been aiming for at the client level is ideally .5-1.5 sec on average it is possible to process larger blocks, but it just causes higher resource requirements sorry, still trying to understand this and i'm not sure if this is actually the case. it seems like the gas target can move completely independently of the base fee I think it means the current voting system remains Full blocks. excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
<@552133098075193354> In my latest PR I changed some variable names per requests and previous discussions.  I went with the ultra verbose and specific:
`max_fee_per_gas` (previously `fee_cap_per_gas`)
`max_inclusion_fee_per_gas` (previously `max_miner_bribe`)
`inclusion_fee_per_gas` (previously `effective_miner_bribe`)
`effective_gas_price` (what `GASPRICE` opcode is set to)
We never did settle on a name, but I think those ones were generally positively received and `bribe` has gotten a lot of hate (and I have been convinced it isn't accurate).

excerpts.author: timbeiko
excerpts.content: Good feedback from the mining channel. What do people think about updating the EIP rationale related to the burning of the base fee?

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: EIPs are technical standards.  It is not appropriate to include arguments in them at all.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: (if such exist now, we should probably remove them)

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Motivation section is a bit of an exception, as we usually allow some *very high level* statements about why someone would want to implement the EIP.  However, it isn't meant to be a constantly updating arguments for/against.
